text_summary.body: In a series of question-and-answer disputations the LORD affirms his love for Jacob against Edom, whose ruins will not be rebuilt; condemns priests who offer blind and lame animals that the governor would refuse; recalls the covenant with Levi; denounces marriage to "the daughter of a foreign god" and faithless divorce; announces his messenger and the Lord's sudden coming to his temple in refining judgment; calls the people robbers for withholding tithes; records the godly in a book of remembrance; and closes with the day that burns like a furnace, the sun of righteousness, the law of Moses and the sending of Elijah.

setting.period: Mid-fifth century BC (after 515; Smith c. 460–445, Keil after 433)
setting.body: The temple is rebuilt and a governor (pechah) receives gifts (1:8). Smith dates the book between about 510 and Nehemiah's reforms, preferring the period just before them because the governor accepts gifts (cf. Neh 5:14–18) and no recent covenant is mentioned. Keil, following Vitringa, dates it after Nehemiah's first term, comparing Mal 2:11 with Neh 13:23 and Mal 3:8–10 with Neh 13:10–14. Guzik places it at or just after Nehemiah's time.

rulers.role: King of Persia (on both main datings)

constraints.subject: evt_01M4W3HPXQKWSTZJ6F477CV1AS
constraints.textual_assertion: You offer polluted bread on my altar … Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse
assumptions: The temple and its service are functioning and the zeal of Haggai and Zechariah has faded (Smith: terminus a quo about 510 BC).

constraints.subject: evt_01M4W3HPXQKWSTZJ6F477CV1AS
constraints.textual_assertion: offer it now to your governor
assumptions: Both main views (just before Nehemiah's reforms, Smith; after Nehemiah's first term, Keil) fall in the reign of Artaxerxes I; see the disputed claim.

terminology.gloss: A provincial governor; Smith notes the title was used widely (Zerubbabel, Nehemiah, Bagoas/Bigvai) and gives no precise date.

"My messenger": a personal name, possibly short for "messenger of the LORD" (Keil), or an editorial title taken from 3:1 for an anonymous book (Smith); the LXX reads "by the hand of his messenger"; the Targum names Ezra the scribe.

competing_reconstructions.label: Just before Nehemiah's reforms (c. 460–445 BC)
competing_reconstructions.summary: Malachi prepared the way for Nehemiah; a gift-taking governor is present and no recent covenant is invoked.

competing_reconstructions.label: During or after Nehemiah's second term (after 433 BC)
proponents: D. Guzik (at or just after Nehemiah's time)
competing_reconstructions.summary: The abuses match those Nehemiah found on his return (Neh 13).

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik reads "Esau I have hated" as non-election rather than emotional hatred.
Guzik sees two messengers in 3:1, the forerunner and Jesus.
